25(OH)D of between 15 and 20 ng mL1 require 100 IUs to raise the blood level by approximately 0.6–1 ng mL1. A multitude
of studies have reported that maintaining a blood concentration of 25(OH)D of at least 30 ng mL1 and ideally as recommended
by the Endocrine Society between 40 and 60 ng mL1 reduces risk of preeclampsia, premature births, autoimmune disorders,
cardiovascular disease, neurocognitive dysfunction including Alzheimer’s disease, type 2 diabetes and infectious diseases (Holick,
2010; Holick et al., 2011; Hossein-nezhad and Holick, 2013; Płudowski et al., 2013; Charoenngam and Holick, 2020). In the era of
COVID 19 several studies have reported signiﬁcant reductions in infectivity, morbidity and mortality associated with this highly
infectious and deadly viral infection (Charoenngam and Holick, 2020; Kaufman et al., 2020, Charoenngam et al., 2021; Seal
et al., 2022). It is unrealistic for most of the world’s population to obtain an adequate amount of vitamin D from dietary sources
and sensible sun exposure. Although in the lay press it is suggested that 5–15 min of sun exposure will produce enough vitamin D,
